headline: The US cigarette tax doubles; Philip Morris challenges Reynolds
text: The federal tax on cigarettes doubled on 1 January, from 8 to 16 cents a pack, the first rise since 1951. Philip Morris, the maker of Marlboro, is challenging R.J. Reynolds for the place of largest US cigarette company. It also owns Miller, which is among the world's biggest brewers.

headline: Schlumberger earned a record $1.3 billion in 1982
text: Schlumberger, the oil services company that measures what is underground for the oil companies, earned a record of about 1.3 billion dollars in 1982. That made it the most profitable of the world's 1,000 largest companies.

headline: Eastern flies the first 757 passengers, Atlanta to Tampa
text: Eastern Air Lines began airline service with the Boeing 757 on 1 January, on the route from Atlanta to Tampa. The British aviation authority certified the plane on 14 January.

headline: Apple's new Lisa has a mouse and costs $9,995
text: Apple introduced the Lisa computer on 19 January. It is controlled with a mouse and pictures on the screen instead of typed commands. It costs 9,995 dollars.

headline: Philip Morris opens a 260 million dollar cigarette plant in North Carolina
text: Philip Morris began production in early January at its new plant in Concord, North Carolina. The 1.8 million square foot factory cost 260 million dollars and starts with 350 workers on one shift. It is meant to employ 2,500 and make about 60 billion cigarettes a year by 1986. About 32,000 people have shown interest in jobs.

headline: The prime rate falls to 10.5%
text: Banks cut their prime rate to 10.5% on 21 February. A year ago, on 18 February 1982, it stood at 17%.

headline: The final episode of M*A*S*H is watched by 121.6 million people
text: The last episode of the TV comedy M*A*S*H aired on 28 February. It drew 121.6 million viewers, the most-watched broadcast in American history to that date.

headline: Venezuela devalues the bolivar on 'Black Friday'
text: On 18 February Venezuela devalued its currency, the bolivar. Oil-exporting countries that borrowed heavily in dollars are struggling as the oil price has fallen.

headline: OPEC cuts its oil price for the first time, to $29
text: On 14 March, after 12 days of talks in London, OPEC cut the official price of oil by 5 dollars to 29 dollars a barrel, the first cut in its history. It also set a ceiling of 17.5 million barrels a day for its members' output. Saudi Arabia will act as the "swing producer", adjusting its output to defend the price.

headline: IBM brings out the PC XT
text: IBM introduced the PC XT (Model 5160) in March, the follow-up model to its original personal computer.

headline: Reagan proposes a missile shield in space
text: On 23 March President Reagan proposed a Strategic Defense Initiative to intercept enemy missiles before they land.

headline: Berkshire's book value rose 40% in 1982
text: In his yearly letter Warren Buffett reported that Berkshire Hathaway's net worth grew by 208 million dollars, or 40%, in 1982, to 737.43 dollars per share. Berkshire owns about 60% of Blue Chip Stamps, and the two firms may merge in 1983. The Buffalo News, which started a Sunday paper six years ago, now sells 367,000 copies on Sundays, 35% more than its rival's 272,000 back then.

headline: Tokyo Disneyland opens, Disney's first park outside America
text: Tokyo Disneyland opened to the public on 15 April. It is the first Disney theme park outside the United States.

headline: The Disney Channel starts on cable TV
text: The Disney Channel began broadcasting on American cable in April. It is a channel devoted to Disney programming.

headline: Wal-Mart opens its first Sam's Club
text: Wal-Mart opened its first Sam's Club in April in Midwest City, Oklahoma. It is a membership warehouse store where people pay a fee to shop for goods in bulk at low prices.

headline: Apple hires John Sculley as its new boss
text: Apple has hired John Sculley, the president of PepsiCo, as its chief executive. Apple, led by young founders until now, is betting that a soft-drink manager can help it sell computers to ordinary people.

headline: Two years in, Jack Welch has cut tens of thousands of jobs at GE
text: Jack Welch became head of General Electric in 1981. In two years he is reported to have cut about 72,000 jobs and closed a dozen factories. His rule is that each GE business must be first or second in its market.

headline: A bomb wrecks the US embassy in Beirut; Challenger flies
text: A bomb killed 63 people at the American embassy in Beirut on 18 April. Earlier, on 4 April, the space shuttle Challenger had flown its first mission.

headline: Michael Jackson moonwalks on live television
text: On a TV special for Motown's anniversary, aired 16 May, Michael Jackson sang "Billie Jean" and did the dance that people now call the moonwalk, for the first time in public.

headline: Return of the Jedi opens, six years after Star Wars
text: Return of the Jedi, the third Star Wars film, opened on 25 May, exactly six years after the first one.

headline: Two labs report a virus that may cause AIDS
text: On 20 May research groups led by Robert Gallo and Luc Montagnier each reported in the journal Science a retrovirus that may cause the new disease AIDS. It is still unproven whether it is the cause.

headline: Thatcher wins a landslide second term
text: Margaret Thatcher's Conservatives were re-elected by a landslide in Britain on 9 June.

headline: Sally Ride becomes the first American woman in space
text: Sally Ride flew on the space shuttle Challenger on 18 June, the first American woman to travel in space.

headline: Motorola's mobile phone goes on sale
text: The Motorola DynaTAC, a handheld mobile telephone, came to market on 13 June.

headline: India beats the West Indies in the cricket World Cup
text: India won the cricket World Cup in England on 25 June, beating the West Indies by 43 runs.

headline: Nintendo's Famicom goes on sale in Japan
text: Nintendo's Famicom, a home video-game machine, went on sale in Japan on 15 July.

headline: Anti-Tamil riots in Sri Lanka
text: After 13 soldiers were killed in an ambush on 23 July, riots against Tamils broke out in Sri Lanka and killed hundreds of people, possibly as many as 3,000.

headline: Poland ends martial law
text: Poland announced on 20 July that martial law is ending, together with an amnesty for political prisoners.

headline: A ten-year-old American girl visits the Soviet Union
text: Samantha Smith, aged ten, flew to Moscow on 7 July at the invitation of Soviet leader Yuri Andropov.

headline: Berkshire Hathaway closes above $1,000 a share for the first time
text: The price of a share of Berkshire Hathaway ended a day above 1,000 dollars for the first time on 26 August. Berkshire has never split its shares, so each one is very expensive.

headline: The prime rate goes up for the first time in a year and a half
text: Banks raised the prime rate from 10.5% to 11% on 8 August. It was the first increase since February 1982.

headline: Benigno Aquino is shot dead in Manila
text: The Philippine opposition leader Benigno Aquino was shot and killed on 21 August, as he returned from exile.

headline: Hurricane Alicia hits Texas
text: Hurricane Alicia struck the Texas coast on 18 August, killing 22 people.

headline: Siemens puts its first commercial MRI scanner into service
text: In August a Siemens MAGNETOM, the company's first commercial MRI machine, went into operation at the Mallinckrodt Institute of Radiology in St. Louis, USA, after just under three months of installation. An MRI scanner uses a huge magnet to take pictures of the inside of the body. Siemens had tested an advanced prototype at Hannover Medical School since February.

headline: The Soviet Union shoots down a Korean airliner
text: On 1 September a Soviet fighter shot down Korean Air Lines Flight 007 near Sakhalin Island, killing all 269 on board, including a US congressman. The Soviet Union admitted the shoot-down on 6 September, saying its pilots did not know it was a passenger plane.

headline: Australia II ends 132 years of American dominance in the America's Cup
text: The yacht Australia II won the America's Cup on 26 September. It was the first time in 132 years that the New York Yacht Club lost the trophy.

headline: Atari buries 700,000 unsold games in the desert
text: About 700,000 unsold Atari cartridges and consoles were buried in a landfill at Alamogordo, New Mexico, on 26 September.

headline: Piquet wins the Formula One title in a BMW-powered car
text: Nelson Piquet became Formula One champion on 15 October at Kyalami, South Africa, winning by two points over Alain Prost. His Brabham had a BMW turbocharged engine, the first title won with turbo power.

headline: Berkshire buys Nebraska Furniture Mart on a handshake
text: Berkshire Hathaway bought 90% of Nebraska Furniture Mart in Omaha, a deal that closed in October. It is reported to have cost about 60 million dollars. The founder, Rose Blumkin, is 89 and keeps working on the sales floor seven days a week; Buffett did not audit her books.

headline: Truck bombs kill 241 US servicemen in Beirut; US troops land in Grenada
text: On 23 October two suicide truck bombs in Beirut killed 241 American servicemen and 58 French paratroopers. Two days later, on 25 October, the United States invaded Grenada.

headline: The first commercial cell phone call is made in Chicago
text: The first call on a commercial cellular network was made in Chicago on 13 October.

headline: The FDA approves Sandoz's anti-rejection drug cyclosporine
text: The US health regulator approved cyclosporine on 14 November. Sandoz sells it as Sandimmune. Sandoz scientists found the fungus that makes it in soil from Norway and Wisconsin and saw in 1972 that it calms the body's immune system, which helps transplanted organs survive.

headline: IBM launches the PCjr, a PC for the home
text: IBM released the PCjr in November. It is aimed at the home market.

headline: The first US cruise missiles arrive in Britain
text: The first US cruise missiles arrived at RAF Greenham Common in England on 13 November, with peace protesters outside. Ronald Reagan became the first US president to speak to Japan's parliament on 11 November.

headline: Martin Luther King Jr. Day becomes a national holiday
text: President Reagan signed the law creating a holiday for Martin Luther King Jr. on 2 November.

headline: The Dow ends 1983 at 1,258.64; inflation is down to about 3%
text: The Dow Jones average finished the year at 1,258.64, up 20.27%. Inflation, which was 10.3% in 1981, is down to about 3%, and unemployment, which peaked at 10.8% a year ago, is falling.

headline: Cabbage Patch Kids dolls cause Christmas fights in the shops
text: Parents fought to get a Cabbage Patch Kids doll for Christmas. Coleco shipped 3.3 million of them in 1983, at 18 to 28 dollars each. One doll was on the cover of Newsweek.

headline: Diet Coke is already the third biggest soft drink in America
text: Diet Coke, launched in July 1982, has overtaken 7UP by the end of 1983 to become the third best-selling soft drink in the United States.

headline: Argentina gets its democracy back
text: On 10 December Raul Alfonsin took office as president of Argentina, ending seven years of military rule.
